column9: Fletcher 2005 Eq. 1 and Fig. 2: pipe diameter d = 1.32 L^0.43 with d and L in millimetres, regression on measured Eastern European panpipes; a Peruvian instrument showed a very similar but much less regular scaling
Fletcher 2005 Eq. 1 (organ flue ranks scale as about 0.75)
Davies, Pinho and English 2006 Eq. 5 limit ka -> 0: end correction of a thin-walled open end 0.6133 radius
Fletcher 2005 Sec. IV: initial jet half-width about 0.5 to 1 mm; the player reduces the lip height 2b0 for high notes (Sec. VI): 1 mm taken for the lowest tube
same source: 0.5 mm taken for the highest tube; tubes between are linear in log2(f)

Fletcher 2005 Sec. IV: jet length typically about 5 to 10 mm, shorter for high notes (Sec. VI). 10 mm is the upper end of that range and was the cut-up of the lowest tube until the cards took the flute-player law of the player-law rows below (D3 now 10.05 mm)
same source: 5 mm is the lower end of that range and was the cut-up of the highest tube until the cards took the flute-player law of the player-law rows below (B4 now 6.30 mm)

Fletcher 1975 Eq. 2 (and Eq. 5): the measured jet length l [mm] = 1.8 + 100 nu^(-1/2), nu in Hz, carries a dead interval of 1.8 mm shielded from the acoustic field; four experienced flute players, all points within about +-20 %; the cut-up of every pan-pipe card at the tube's equal-tempered pitch (D3 10.05 mm to B4 6.30 mm); a FLUTE law applied to a stopped pipe by analogy (u-player-controls)
same source, Eq. 2: the coefficient of nu^(-1/2) in mm Hz^(1/2)

Fletcher 1975 Eq. 1: the median blowing pressure in excess of atmospheric p [mbar] = 0.008 nu, nu in Hz, four flute players (scatter mostly +-50 %), measured by a 1 mm catheter in the lip corner, plotted from C4 (262 Hz) to about C7; the blowing pressure of every pan-pipe card at the tube's equal-tempered pitch (117.5 Pa at D3 to 395.1 Pa at B4, 1 mbar = 100 Pa); D3 lies below every pitch reported and G3 only at the alto flute's lowest note, which the text covers without data (u-player-controls)

Fletcher 2005 Eq. 6 with alpha about 2 and gamma about 0.4: in a STOPPED pipe the steady entrained flow is blocked, so the jet midplane is deflected outside the lip by about 0.5 of the jet half-width (typically 0.5 mm for a low note); depends on the player and note
Fletcher 2005 Eq. 9: epsilon about 0.1 (6 degrees); NOT modelled by the generic flue input, which keeps the initial half-width (u-jet-spreading)
